What is the theoretical fastest a computer chip can go?

that's a really complex question because it matters what kind of operation the computer is performing and whether you care about the amount of actual work completed or just mean the speed of a processor. If you mean the actual clock speed then the fastest currently available is at 8.429 GHz. For an answer to what the theoretical limit is you would have to reduce the gate delay and address the problem of heat generated by the processor. So the answer is a sort of we don't really know at this point but we've already hit the wall where processors don't get too much faster.

Now if you're concerned about the amount of work done then it matters heavily how dependent your data set and operations being performed on the data is. Parallelism in computing allows for multiple threads to be programmed and process data simultaneously which can for many applications even running at a slower speed then the above cited bulldozer core still get more work done in less time. Think of it kinda like having 8 really slow guys building a deck as opposed to one really fast expert carpenter. Unless the carpenter is 8 times faster than the average slow guy, then the slow guys will get done first, effectively making them the faster. this is why chip manufacturers don't brag about processor speed as much as they did in the past and the big seller has been the number of cores: dual, quad, 8 (should be octo cause that sounds cooler) and so on. Parallel cores do have lots of issues though such as synchronization, data-transport issues, and parallel programming tools are getting better but are still not to the ease of use compared to programming a single chip.

TL;DR depends on how you define fastest, we're already really close to the fastest but parallel architectures in computers allow for more work to be done in shorter time periods, making them effectively faster.

we've already hit the wall where processors don't get too much faster

Not really, unless you just mean clock speed. There are other ways to make things faster, but traditionally just upping the clock speed was the simplest way to make them faster.

No, you can't. The Landauer limit won't let you. For each and every irreversible operation, you are generating entropy. You're generating about kT ln2 of heat per irreversible bit operation at an operating temperature of T.
